input.name: image
input.preprocessing: whole photo, EXIF-rotated upright, resized (squeezed) to 224x224 bilinear, divide by 255; normalisation is inside the model

outputs.probs: softmax over the 15 classes, shape [1, 15]; add front + back for the note value

speaking.rule: speak the top value if it is not 'none' and its probability >= threshold (the app also needs 3 frames in a row)
speaking.threshold_chosen_on: lowest threshold with <= 0.2% (1 in 500) wrong-value rate on 4 augmented passes of the validation set

faq.question: What is the Pakistani Banknote Reader?
faq.answer: A free web app for blind and low-vision people in Pakistan. You point a phone camera at a banknote and it says the value out loud in Urdu or English. It runs in the browser, so there is no app to install.

faq.question: How do I use it?
faq.answer: Open https://boltanote.vercel.app in a phone browser, tap Start camera, and hold a note in front of the camera. It says the value as soon as it is sure. With no camera, you can upload a photo or tap a test photo.

faq.question: Which Pakistani notes can it read?
faq.answer: All seven notes in circulation: Rs 10, 20, 50, 100, 500, 1,000 and 5,000, front or back, including folded or upside down. It knows the 2005–2008 designs, not the State Bank's new series.

faq.question: Is it free, and does it need an account?
faq.answer: It is free, with no account and no install. The code is open source under the MIT licence.

faq.question: Does it work offline?
faq.answer: Yes, after the first visit. The model, the runtime and the voice clips are saved on the phone, so it keeps working and reopens with no internet.

faq.question: Are my camera pictures uploaded anywhere?
faq.answer: No. Every picture is processed on the phone, inside the browser. Nothing is sent to a server.

faq.question: How accurate is it?
faq.answer: It names the value correctly on 100.0% of 727 unseen photos from the same dataset, and 92.1% of 63 photos taken by other people. On those 63 photos it spoke no wrong amount and stayed silent on 8. The first number mostly shows how alike the dataset's photos are; the second is closer to real use, but 63 photos is a small test.

faq.question: When does it stay silent?
faq.answer: It speaks only when it is at least 68% sure and three frames in a row agree, because saying a wrong amount is worse than saying nothing. The 0.68 threshold keeps wrong answers to at most 1 in 500 on a stress test of 2,940 hard, augmented validation photos.

faq.question: Does it work with screen readers?
faq.answer: It is built for them: results are announced to TalkBack and VoiceOver through a live region, every control is a large button, and on Android it also vibrates a code for each note. It has not yet been tested with blind users; that is the next step.

faq.question: Can it detect counterfeit notes?
faq.answer: No. It reads the value of a note and does not check whether the note is genuine. It also reads only one note at a time.

faq.question: Which model does it use?
faq.answer: MobileNetV3-Large, pretrained on ImageNet and fine-tuned to 15 classes: seven notes, front and back, plus "no note". It runs with ONNX Runtime Web and takes about 15 ms per photo on a CPU. It was compared with a CNN trained from scratch and MobileNetV4.

faq.question: What data was it trained on?
faq.answer: The Pakistan Image Currency Dataset (CC0) of 3,611 phone photos, plus 1,000 Imagenette photos for the "no note" class. A hash check found 339 of 402 photos in a second public dataset were near-copies of the first, so only the 63 new ones were used as the external test.

faq.question: Who made it?
faq.answer: Hassan Ali Mehdi, as a Deep Learning semester project at Superior University, Lahore (BSCS-7A), under Dr. Munir Ahmad, November 2026.

faq.question: Where are the code, weights and report?
faq.answer: The code, weights and data splits are at https://github.com/Hassan-Ali-Mehdi-3024/boltanote, and the report is at https://boltanote.vercel.app/report.pdf. Every link, with its alternate, is in the links section of this page.
